hints: Under $x=3\tan\theta$, transform both the differential and the denominator: $dx=3\sec^2\theta d\theta$ and $9+x^2=9\sec^2\theta$.
Substitute these throughout $\dfrac{27}{(9+x^2)^2}dx$ and cancel the numerical and secant factors.
Convert the endpoints separately: $x=0$ gives $\theta=0$, while $x=3$ gives $\tan\theta=1$.
Use $1/\sec^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$ to reach the stated integral with its new limits.
walkthrough:
Differentiate the substitution $x = 3\tan\theta$ with respect to $\theta$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = 3\sec^2\theta \implies \mathrm{d}x = 3\sec^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Substitute $x = 3\tan\theta$ into the expression $9 + x^2$:
$$9 + x^2 = 9 + (3\tan\theta)^2 = 9 + 9\tan^2\theta = 9(1 + \tan^2\theta)$$
Apply the trigonometric identity $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$:
$$9 + x^2 = 9\sec^2\theta$$
Square this result to obtain the denominator:
$$(9 + x^2)^2 = (9\sec^2\theta)^2 = 81\sec^4\theta$$

Substitute the numerator $27$, the transformed denominator $81\sec^4\theta$, and $\mathrm{d}x = 3\sec^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$ into the integral:
$$\dfrac{27}{(9 + x^2)^2}\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{27}{81\sec^4\theta} \cdot 3\sec^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \dfrac{81\sec^2\theta}{81\sec^4\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sec^2\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \cos^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Transform the limits of integration from $x$ to $\theta$ using $\tan\theta = \dfrac{x}{3}$:
Lower limit: when $x = 0$, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{0}{3} = 0 \implies \theta = 0$
Upper limit: when $x = 3$, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{3} = 1 \implies \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

Assemble the transformed definite integral with the new limits:
$$I = \int_0^{\pi/4} \cos^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

hints: Use the result of part (a) and the identity $\cos^2\theta=\frac12(1+\cos2\theta)$.
Integrate to obtain an antiderivative containing both a $\theta$ term and a $\sin2\theta$ term.
Evaluate this antiderivative exactly at $\theta=\pi/4$ and $\theta=0$, keeping $\pi$ symbolic.
walkthrough:
Use the cosine double-angle formula $\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1$ to rewrite $\cos^2\theta$ in an integrable form:
$$\cos^2\theta = \dfrac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2\theta$$

Substitute this identity into the integral $I$ from part (a):
$$I = \int_0^{\pi/4} \left( \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2\theta \right)\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Integrate each term with respect to $\theta$:
$$\int \dfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\theta$$
$$\int \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 2\theta$$
Thus the antiderivative is:
$$\left[ \dfrac{1}{2}\theta + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 2\theta \right]_0^{\pi/4}$$

Evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin\!\left(2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{8} + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{8} + \dfrac{1}{4}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{8} + \dfrac{1}{4}$$

Evaluate the antiderivative at the lower limit $\theta = 0$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}(0) + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin(0) = 0 + 0 = 0$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value and write as a single factored expression:
$$I = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{8} + \dfrac{1}{4}\right) - 0 = \dfrac{\pi + 2}{8} = \dfrac{1}{8}(\pi + 2)$$
